findings.issue: Two risks in one entry: the acronym OO must be read as letters (/ˌəʊ ˈəʊ/), not as a word or a long /uː/; and 'object' here is the noun (/ˈɒbdʒɪkt/), not the verb /əbˈdʒekt/.
findings.context: Object orientation (OO) helps you group data and actions together.

findings.issue: The acronym OA should be spelled out as /ˌəʊ ˈeɪ/; a generic reader may treat it as a single token or skip it.
findings.context: Office automation (OA) can print and file documents for you.

findings.issue: The acronym PC must be read as two letters /ˌpiː ˈsiː/, not as a word; a generic reader may also read the brackets aloud.
findings.context: My personal computer (PC) at home runs both games and code.

findings.issue: The acronym TXT is a file-extension spelling and must be read letter by letter /ˌtiː eks ˈtiː/; standalone 'TXT' has no natural word reading.
findings.context: Save the log as plain text (TXT) so every tool can read it.

findings.issue: The acronym IT must be read as letters /ˌaɪ ˈtiː/, not as the pronoun 'it' /ɪt/; this is the main ambiguity in the entry.
findings.context: Popular IT education helps beginners use computers with confidence.

findings.issue: A verb/noun heteronym by stress only: the meaning 进程 is the noun, so stress falls first. A reader could produce the verb /prəˈses/.
findings.context: A process is a program that is running on the computer.

findings.issue: The bracketed '[computer]' is an editorial qualifier, not part of the spoken term; reading the brackets or the qualifier aloud would break the recording. Also note US 'program' vs UK 'programme' spelling, same pronunciation.
findings.context: This program [computer] prints a report every morning.

findings.issue: The acronym QR must be read as letters /ˌkjuː ˈɑː/; the capital 'C' in 'Code' also signals an inconsistent spelling style but does not change pronunciation.
findings.context: The quick response (QR) Code on the poster opens the menu.

findings.issue: 'read' is a heteronym: here it is the present form /riːd/, not the past /red/. ROM is a word-like acronym pronounced /rɒm/, not spelled out.
findings.context: The firmware is stored in read-only memory (ROM) on the board.

findings.issue: 'record' is a stress heteronym: as an attributive noun here it takes first-syllable stress, not the verb /rɪˈkɔːd/.
findings.context: Each record type in the database stores one kind of data.

findings.issue: The bracketed '[cybersecurity]' is a domain qualifier, not spoken text; a generic reader would verbalize it and the brackets.
findings.context: A red team [cybersecurity] tries to break into the system on purpose.

result.notes: All 155 entries (751–905) were checked; every phonetic field is empty, so no IPA could be compared against supplied transcriptions or audio (none was provided) — the IPA above is proposed intended pronunciation. Not flagged, deliberately: ordinary UK/US spelling and vowel variants (normalisation, optical fibre, on-line/online, program/programme), and single-rendering words with no homograph risk. Shared but unrepeated issues: id 844 'process re-engineering' has the same noun-stress requirement as 843; ids 764 and 766 use 'object' as the noun unambiguously, so no finding was raised. Homophones worth knowing but not errors: pharming ≈ farming (814). Spelling consistency only: 'on-line' (774, 775) coexists with 'online' (776–778) — pick one style so recordings and cards match. Meaning note outside pronunciation scope: 777 'online finance' is glossed 网上贷款 (lending), which is narrower than 'finance'; the gloss, not the pronunciation, should be reviewed.
